sentences.text: Labrujasuchus is known from a partial associated skeleton that includes forelimb material, vertebrae, hindlimb parts, and elements of the pubic region.
Its anatomy closely resembles that of the North American shuvosaurids Effigia and Shuvosaurus.
A large internal tuberosity on the humerus, sometimes called a medial process, distinguishes it from related taxa.
The humeral head is teardrop-shaped rather than the D-shape seen in some relatives.
The ischium bears a hypertrophied ventral crest that makes the bone deeper than it is wide, unlike other North American shuvosaurids.
An anterior groove on the fibula, situated just medial to the iliofibularis trochanter, serves as another distinguishing feature.
The holotype skeleton of Labrujasuchus was discovered in 2006 at the Hayden Quarry in Ghost Ranch, New Mexico.
It comes from paleochannel H2, which is dated to approximately 211 million years ago, placing it in the mid-Norian age of the Late Triassic.
Additional material, including a left coracoid from channel H3 and a left tibia from channel H4, has been referred to the genus.
The type locality lies within the Chinle Formation, a widespread Late Triassic deposit in the United States.

Labrujasuchus was described as a new genus and new species by Turner and colleagues, with a long author list that includes Alan H. Turner, Ciara E. Kernan, Adam Laing, Adam C. Pritchard, Michelle R. Stocker, Randall B. Irmis, Nathan D. Smith, Sarah Werning, and Sterling J. Nesbitt.
The genus is named Labrujasuchus, and the species epithet is expectatus.
It is placed within the family Shuvosauridae, which belongs to the superfamily Poposauroidea.
A phylogenetic analysis by Turner et al. excluded the coeval shuvosaurid Sonselasuchus, which had been named two months earlier, from the same clade as Labrujasuchus.
